newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parties anxiously await Hesse vote outcome.
newsitem.headline: German parties anxiously await Hesse vote outcome.

text.p: Germany's political parties anxiously awaited the outcome of a local election in the state of Hesse on Sunday that is this year's main test of voter reaction to high unemployment and wrangling over tax reforms.

The election of local councils throughout Hesse, including the city parliament of Germany's banking capital, Frankfurt, started at 0700 GMT in sunny spring weather which the mainstream parties hope will boost the turnout.
Political leaders have attached such importance to the vote that they have descended on the state en masse in recent weeks.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens have exhorted voters to punish Chancellor Helmut Kohl for failing to stem a surge in joblessness which hit 4.66 million in January -- a level last seen when Adolf Hitler came to power and which has rattled Germans' confidence in a secure future.

Kohl, whose coalition is squabbling with the SPD over plans for urgently needed tax reforms, himself attended a campaign rally in Frankfurt and has said the vote will provide an important signal for the next general election in 1998.

A recent opinion poll published last Friday showed Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU), its Bavarian sister party CSU and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) would have lost their majority in the Bundestag or lower house of the federal parliament if a general election had been held last weekend.

Hesse's polling stations close at 1700 GMT and first computer projections are expected from 1730 GMT. Some 180,000 citizens from other European Union countries living in the state are eligible to vote for the first time.

While opinion pollsters believe the vote will at best give a distorted picture of political sentiment in Germany, politicians have given the elections such prominence that they are bound to have a nationwide relevance.
"Turn the local election into a settling of accounts for the unfair policies of Kohl's government," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine told a party gathering in Hesse's capital, Wiesbaden, last week.
But recent polls show that despite Kohl's problems at the national level, his CDU will gain in the election to Frankfurt's parliament while the SPD will emerge as losers.

A poll by the Mannheim-based Ipos institute published last Sunday put CDU support in Frankfurt at 37 percent, up from 33.4 percent in the last local election in 1993, due mainly to the popularity of the city's CDU mayor Petra Roth.
The SPD is shown falling to 28.0 percent from 32.0 percent while the Greens are the biggest gainers, rising to 19 percent from 14.0 percent.

The FDP, led in Frankfurt by German Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis, are expected to enter Frankfurt's town hall for the first time in 16 years with a vote of six percent, up from 4.4 percent in 1993 which was below the minimum of five percent required to take office.

The far right Republicans are expected to lose ground but will remain in parliament with six percent of the vote, down from 9.3 percent last time. The mainstream parties have said they would not enter a coalition with the Republicans.
It was unclear, however, whether the CDU would obtain the votes needed to stake a claim in government in Frankfurt.

In Hesse overall, the SPD was the strongest party in the last local elections in 1993 with a 36.4 percent share of the vote, followed by the CDU with 32.0 percent, the Greens with 11.0 percent and the FDP with 5.1 percent.
